content.thinking:
The user wants a conceptual answer, so I'll keep it short and plain. Anchors do exist on every fact record, but the brief's JSON projection strips them on purpose to keep the packet compact, and the test checks that "provenance" never leaks, so brief consumers never saw them. The precedent section is a curated, filtered view instead: top-ranked facts only, deduplicated, degraded when transcripts are missing, and checked against disk, and it takes the place of the history.

I'm noting that the precedent section stands in for the history search arm, which COR-2308 removes, so the lookup replaces a second search system over the 263k records. Raw anchors are noisy, with duplicates and stale transcript paths, so the checked, deduplicated rendering is what gets surfaced instead.

content.text:
Good question — the anchors do already exist on every fact record. The precedent section exists because brief readers never actually saw them, and the raw form is not usable as-is.

Three reasons:

1. **Brief deliberately strips raw provenance.** The `--json` packet is byte-budgeted, so `brainBriefJSONFact` carries only id, paths, kind, locus, text, and confidence. A test (`TestBrainBriefJSONProjectionOmitsFollowUpDetail`) enforces that the raw `provenance` field never leaks into the packet. So an agent that read a brief had no path back to the source session.

2. **Raw anchors are noisy and unverified.** A fact often has duplicate anchors: a bare `{session, commit, checkpoint}` next to the same source with a transcript path, or several anchors to one transcript. And a transcript path is only a claim — the file can be absent on this machine (synced facts, pruned sessions). The precedent section dedupes, keeps the transcript pointer only when the file really exists in the brain, and degrades to a session/commit reference when it does not.

3. **It replaces the history search arm.** Today, brief answers "where did this knowledge come from" with a second, independent search system (FTS over ~263k transcript records). The recorded decision (2026-11-09) is that memories are the single retrieval surface. The precedent section gives the same answer — "open this transcript at this line for the full story" — as a lookup over the facts the brief already ranked, with no search and no index. COR-2308 then removes the history arm.

So: the anchors are the data, and precedent is the curated view of that data at the moment an agent needs it — ranked facts only, deduplicated, and checked against disk.

content.text:
It is never built or rebuilt — there is nothing stored. The section is computed fresh inside every `entire brain brief` run and discarded with the packet.

The sequence per brief call:

1. `factstore.Load` reads the fact store (this load already happens for the facts section).
2. `rankFacts` picks the top facts — at most 6 (`brainBriefFactsLimit`), fewer with a smaller `--limit`.
3. `brainBriefPrecedents` walks those facts' anchor lists, which are already in memory, and renders the sources.

The only work beyond pure in-memory iteration is the transcript existence check: for each anchor with a transcript path, the containment guard does one `Lstat` per path component (a transcript path has 3) plus one final `Lstat`, and the helper runs twice per anchor (dedupe pre-pass + render pass). With 6 facts and a few anchors each, that is on the order of 100–200 `Lstat` calls worst case — microseconds to low single-digit milliseconds on a local disk. It does not register next to the rest of brief (fact load, BM25, and today still the history FTS).

Nothing happens at commit or checkpoint time for this section, and there is no cache to invalidate. That is the point of the design: the history arm it replaces needs an index built and kept fresh over ~263k records; precedent is a per-request lookup over at most 6 records, so "when is it rebuilt" stops being a question anyone has to ask.

The follow-up is up: https://entire.com/gh/entireio/-/trails/2816

- Verified before push: precedent tests green, `gofmt -s` and `go vet` clean.

One side effect to be aware of: `main` is checked out in your primary repo folder, so my `git checkout main` here failed and the subsequent pull fast-forwarded the old `evisdren/cor-2307-work` branch to main's tip instead. That branch was already merged, so nothing is lost — it just now points at the merge commit locally.

This workspace is now on the new branch, so Conductor will show trail change 498. Merge it through the trail when you are happy with it.
